summary:
## Background
Risperidone is primarily metabolized by CYP2D6. In children, adverse events (AEs) from risperidone are common, but the impact of CYP2D6 genetic variation on AE risk has been unclear. This retrospective cohort study (n=257, ≤18 years old, ≥4 weeks of risperidone) examined whether CYP2D6 metabolizer status predicts AEs.

## Key Findings
- CYP2D6 poor or intermediate metabolizers (PM/IM; 13%, n=33) had a higher AE rate than normal or ultrarapid metabolizers (NM/UM; 87%, n=224): 46% vs 27% (P=0.04).
- After adjustment for age, sex, race, and initial dose, PM/IM status was associated with increased AE risk: adjusted OR 2.4 (95% CI 1.1–5.1; P=0.03).
- Overall, 30% of children experienced AEs; most common were weight change (9%), sedation (6%), and extrapyramidal symptoms (6%).
- Among NM/UM patients, concomitant strong CYP2D6 inhibitors did not significantly change AE risk (adjusted OR 1.2; 95% CI 0.4–3.3; P=0.7), suggesting genotype was a stronger predictor than drug–drug inhibition in this cohort.
- The ultrarapid group was small (n=6); 50% had AEs, but numbers were insufficient for firm conclusions.

## Clinical Implications
- Children with reduced CYP2D6 function (PM/IM) are at higher risk of risperidone AEs. If CYP2D6 results are available, consider:
  - Alternative antipsychotic therapy, or
  - Lower starting doses with slow titration and enhanced monitoring for metabolic and movement-related AEs.
- Pre-prescription CYP2D6 genotyping can help identify high-risk patients and tailor therapy, although formal dosing guidelines for risperidone by CYP2D6 genotype are not yet established.
- Maintain routine AE surveillance for all pediatric patients on risperidone; be especially vigilant in those with known reduced CYP2D6 activity.
